must: **Moore's Law**: transistor count doubles every ~18–24 months. It's **clock speed** that stopped rising (~2005), not transistor count.
**Power wall**: P ∝ C·V²·f. Higher f needs higher V, and V is squared → heat explodes.
**Multi-core (CMP)** = several cores on one die/socket. **Hyper-Threading** = 2 threads sharing one core (not 2× speed).
Three parallel machines: **Cluster** (many PCs + network), **SMP** (many CPUs, one memory), **CMP** (many cores, one chip).
**Parallel** = faster execution, fine grain, tightly coupled, homogeneous. **Distributed** = resource sharing/throughput, coarse grain, loosely coupled, heterogeneous.
Motivations: performance, price/performance, technology limits, inherently parallel apps, sharing, availability, incremental growth, **scavenging** (~25% utilisation).
formulas: 2 cores @ f/2, V/2: P = 2C·(V/2)²·(f/2) = **¼** of 1 core @ f, same work
traps: Saying Moore's Law 'ended' because CPUs stopped getting faster — it's about transistor count.
Treating Hyper-Threading as extra cores: 8 logical processors on a 4-core HT chip = 4 real cores.
Mixing up grain sizes: parallel = **fine**, distributed = **coarse**.
likely: Why did manufacturers move to multi-core? (power/heat, design complexity, multithreaded apps)
Compare parallel vs distributed computing (goal, grain, architecture).
Machine A vs B cost question: time → cost → value of time saved → choose and justify.
tricks: Multi-core reasons = **'Hot, Hard, Already threaded'**: heat, hard to design, apps already multithreaded.

story.problem: Single-core CPUs hit the power wall: a faster clock means too much heat.
story.fix: Put many cores on one chip and many machines on a network: parallel and distributed computing.
story.next: More hardware alone isn't enough. How do we know going parallel actually pays off?

terms.def: Transistors per chip double roughly every 18–24 months.
The limit on clock speed caused by power ∝ C·V²·f turning into heat.
Chip Multi-Processor: several cores on one die, in one socket.
Intel's SMT: two hardware threads sharing one core's execution units.
Symmetric Multi-Processor: several CPUs sharing one memory.
Many whole computers joined by a fast network and used together.
How much work a task does between communications (fine vs coarse).
Using idle computers' wasted cycles for useful work.
